summary: A landlocked country in the Great Lakes region of East Africa, called the 'Land of a Thousand Hills'; it rebuilt after the genocide tragedy of 1994 and is known for good public safety and economic development.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was introduced by the White Fathers in 1900, when Rwanda was part of German East Africa; from 1916 it was ruled by Belgium. The Belgian colonial authorities cooperated with the Catholic Church and used mission schools to train a Tutsi elite; in 1931 Belgium deposed King Musinga, who was unwilling to be baptized, and installed the baptized Mutara III, and in 1946 the king even dedicated the country to Christ, so Catholicism became the largest religion. But in the 1994 genocide some clergy were implicated and churches became sites of massacres, damaging the Church's prestige, and the share of followers has fallen from more than sixty percent in the past.

ranking.name: Pentecostalism
ranking.description: Pentecostalism has grown rapidly since the genocide of 1994, as many survivors and refugees returning from Uganda and Congo came into contact with charismatic churches during exile. After the genocide the credibility of the Catholic Church was damaged, and Pentecostalism attracted large numbers of followers with a message emphasizing forgiveness, healing and personal rebirth, especially in cities such as Kigali.

ranking.name: Other Protestant (Anglican, Baptist, etc.)
ranking.description: Other Protestants include Anglicans, Baptists and Presbyterians, first introduced during the German period (from 1907) by German Lutheran missionaries and taken over after World War I by Belgian Protestant missions. In the 1930s the East African Revival began at an Anglican mission station in Rwanda and spread throughout East Africa, with far-reaching influence.

ranking.name: Seventh-day Adventist Church
ranking.description: The Seventh-day Adventist Church arrived in Rwanda in 1919 and established schools and hospitals in the west and south, attracting followers through education and medical care. Rwanda is one of the countries with the highest proportion of Adventists in the world.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam was brought in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by Swahili traders from the East African coast, and Muslims are concentrated in districts of Kigali such as Nyamirambo. During the 1994 genocide many Muslims protected and sheltered Tutsi, and after the genocide the image of Islam improved and attracted some converts, but the proportion is still only about 2%.

religion.background: Rwandans traditionally believed in the supreme god Imana and in ancestral spirits. The White Fathers arrived in 1900, and during the Belgian colonial period Catholicism became the state religion, with the Church closely bound up with politics. The genocide of 1994 caused about eight hundred thousand deaths, and the involvement of some Church figures in the killings severely damaged the prestige of Catholicism. After the genocide Pentecostalism and other Protestant groups grew rapidly, and Christians as a whole still make up more than ninety percent of the population.

language.official: The official languages are Kinyarwanda, English, French and Swahili.

ranking.name: Kinyarwanda
ranking.description: Kinyarwanda belongs to the Bantu branch and is the shared mother tongue of the Hutu, Tutsi and Twa of Rwanda. Unlike many African countries, Rwanda was a linguistically unified kingdom before colonization, with all groups speaking the same language, so almost the entire population speaks Kinyarwanda as their mother tongue. After 1994 the government stressed the national identity of 'we are all Rwandans', and Kinyarwanda is an important bond uniting the various groups.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English rose greatly in status after the 1994 genocide, because many members of the Tutsi-led Rwandan Patriotic Front had grown up in exile in English-speaking Uganda. In 2008 the government announced that education would switch to English as the main language of instruction in place of French, and in 2009 Rwanda joined the Commonwealth. Today English is the main working language of government and business, but very few people speak it as their mother tongue.

language.history: Kinyarwanda has been the common language of the Kingdom of Rwanda for hundreds of years; it had no writing before the German colonization of the late 19th century, and missionaries recorded it in the Latin alphabet. During Belgian rule of 1916–1962 French became the language of administration and education, while Swahili was used in commerce. After the genocide of 1994, large numbers of refugees who had grown up in Uganda returned and English rose in status, from 2008 education switched mainly to English, and in 2017 Swahili also became an official language.

ranking.name: Isombe (cassava leaf stew)
ranking.description: Pounded cassava leaves are stewed with eggplant, spinach and onions, with peanut butter or palm oil added, sometimes with dried fish or meat, giving a creamy texture with a nutty aroma.
ranking.history: Cassava originated in South America, was introduced to Africa by the Portuguese after the 16th century, and reached Rwanda in the 19th and 20th centuries. To prevent famine, the Belgian colonial authorities once forced farmers to plant drought-tolerant crops such as cassava. Cassava leaf stew is quite common in the Great Lakes region of Rwanda, Congo and Burundi, is an everyday family side dish, and often appears at wedding and festival banquets.

ranking.name: Brochettes (grilled skewers)
ranking.description: Pieces of goat, beef or fish are skewered, marinated in spices and grilled over charcoal, often served with fried potatoes, fried plantains and chili sauce; it is the most common food in Rwandan bars.
ranking.history: 'Brochette' is the French word for a meat skewer, and the name reflects the French influence left by Belgian colonial rule. In Rwanda, grilled goat skewers are the most popular accompaniment to drinks in bars and restaurants, often paired with local Primus beer or banana beer. Sitting together eating brochettes when friends gather at weekends is one of the most important social settings in Rwandan urban life.

ranking.name: Boiled green bananas (ibitoke)
ranking.description: Green cooking bananas are peeled and steamed or boiled, or stewed with tomato, onion and meat, giving a soft, starchy texture similar to potato with a slight sweetness.
ranking.history: Bananas originated in Southeast Asia and reached the Great Lakes region of East Africa more than a thousand years ago, and in Rwanda, with its fertile volcanic soil, they have become one of the most important crops. Rwandans not only treat bananas as a staple but also use them to brew traditional banana beer (urwagwa), drunk at weddings, festivals and tribal ceremonies. Banana groves are also an important part of the Rwandan rural landscape.

ranking.name: Ubugali (stiff porridge)
ranking.description: Cassava flour or cornmeal is poured into boiling water and stirred constantly, cooked into a thick paste that can be pinched up by hand, and eaten with bean stew, cassava leaf stew or meat broth.
ranking.history: Ubugali is a common staple in Rwanda and throughout East Africa, sharing its origin with East Africa's ugali. Cassava and maize are both American crops that became widespread only in the colonial period. Because it is filling and cheap, it is the everyday staple of rural Rwandans and urban working families, and a common dish in school lunches.

ranking.name: Mandazi (fried dough)
ranking.description: A dough kneaded from flour, sugar, coconut milk or milk and yeast is cut into triangles or rounds and deep-fried, with a soft, lightly sweet texture, often eaten for breakfast with milky tea.
ranking.history: Mandazi originated on the Swahili coast of East Africa and was brought inland by Muslim traders and migrants along the caravan routes of the 19th century. In Rwanda it is the most common street and near-school breakfast snack, and it is cheap. Rwandans have a habit of drinking milky tea, which is related to the local highland tea plantations, tea being one of Rwanda's most important export crops, and mandazi with milky tea has become an everyday breakfast combination.
